text: Service Level Management as an ITIL concept is a target response or resolution time. Implementing it on the platform means building an SLA Definition, stored on the contract_sla table — and the duration field is the easy part.

The real implementation work sits underneath the duration: four condition builders called Applies To, Start, Pause, Stop, and Reset. Get the duration right and the conditions wrong, and the SLA produces a precise-looking number that measures nothing real.

Applies To decides which records this definition attaches to at all — typically incident where Priority is 1. Start, Pause, Stop, and Reset are independent condition builders that control exactly when that attached record's clock begins, suspends, ends, or restarts.

The Start condition deserves the most attention. Starting the clock on record creation sounds intuitive, but if a Priority 1 incident sits in a queue for ten minutes before anyone picks it up, that queue time gets baked into the resolution clock before an agent has even touched the ticket.

Many real implementations instead start the SLA when State moves to In Progress, or when assigned_to is first populated — the point work genuinely began. A Start condition built on the wrong field doesn't introduce a small error; it changes what the SLA is actually measuring.

An SLA Definition is a template. When a real record satisfies Applies To and Start, the platform creates a task_sla record — one running instance tracking that specific record's elapsed time, percentage consumed, and breach status.
Next up: SLA Workflows. We'll follow that task_sla instance through Pause, Stop, and what actually happens if the clock runs out before Stop fires — including the real Awaiting Caller pause case.
